title: Hosea
subtitle: a prophet of the north, a marriage, and a love that will not let go
lead: Hosea is the first of the Twelve, the short prophets the Hebrew Bible counts as one scroll, and the only prophet with a book who came from the northern kingdom. He spoke in the last decades before Assyria ended that kingdom in 722 BC, when Israel was rich, then in chaos, and then under foreign rule. His book opens with the strangest command given to any prophet: marry a wife of prostitution, and name the children Jezreel, Not Shown Compassion and Not My People. It closes with a call to return and a picture of the LORD as dew.

What holds the fourteen chapters together is a love that is not returned. The LORD is a husband whose wife credits her lovers with his gifts, a father who taught his son to walk, a healer who is treated as a moth, a lion and a baker's oven all at once. The book's Hebrew is among the hardest in the Bible, and the Plain English Translation says plainly where it follows a reading other than the Masoretic Text, where the Greek is different, and where nobody knows. It also keeps Hosea's words for sex and betrayal plain, for his unsparing language is part of what he means.
facts: Hosea son of Beeri (1:1); how much of the book is his own words and how much was added is debated
About 755 to 725 BC, in the reigns of Jeroboam II and the last kings of Israel; the heading also names Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah
The northern kingdom (Israel, Ephraim, Samaria), Judah, the Assyrian rise under Tiglath-pileser III and the fall of Samaria in 722 BC (the year 721 has also been argued)
Prophetic oracles in poetry, with two prose narratives of the prophet's marriage (1:2-9 and 3:1-5)
Hebrew, with many rare and uncertain words; the Greek translation, the Dead Sea scrolls 4QXIIc, 4QXIId and 4QXIIg (parts only) and the Masoretic Text are the main witnesses

The Plain English Translation uses English (KJV) numbers. The Hebrew Bible numbers 1:10-11 as 2:1-2 (so Hebrew chapter 2 is 2:3-25), 11:12 as 12:1 and 13:16 as 14:1; every note gives the English number
First of the Twelve Prophets in the Hebrew and the Greek order; in the Hebrew Bible one of the Latter Prophets, in Christian Bibles one of the Minor Prophets

audience.to: The people of the northern kingdom of Israel, called Ephraim after its leading tribe and Samaria after its capital: the royal court, the priests of Bethel, Gilgal and the other shrines, the landowners, and ordinary Israelites at the festivals. Some oracles turn to Judah (4:15; 5:5, 10, 12, 14; 6:4, 11), but the book's first hearers lived in Jeroboam II's peace and the chaos that followed, when kings were murdered and Assyria took the north in stages.
audience.why: To tell a people who believed in the LORD and in the covenant that their worship, their treaties and their politics were a form of unfaithfulness, and that the LORD's love could not be cancelled by it. The marriage and the names of the children put the message in a family; the lawsuit puts it in court; the history of Jacob and the exodus puts it in memory. After 722 BC the book was kept and edited in Judah, so its second audience was the survivors who needed to know why the north fell and whether the LORD had finished with them.
views: Hosea spoke to Israel in its last decades, including the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (735-732 BC). This is the common view of the oracles themselves.

The book was gathered and expanded in Judah as a warning and a hope: the added references to Judah (1:7, 11; 3:5; 4:15; 12:2) and the hopeful endings point to this audience. Many critical scholars hold that this is how the book got its present form.
Jews who read Hosea 14 before Yom Kippur and Hosea 2 before Shavuot, and Christians who heard in it the calling of the Gentiles and Christ's love for the church, took the words as their own.

authorship: Hosea wrote or spoke the whole book. The Talmud says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote down the Twelve (Bava Batra 15a). Jerome and the church fathers treat the book as Hosea's own.

Hans Walter Wolff proposed that the book grew in stages: Hosea's own sayings, then collections made by a circle of his followers, then later editing in Judah. Others (Andersen and Freedman, Stuart, Garrett) hold that more of the book goes back to Hosea himself. Judean additions, such as 1:7 and 3:5, are discussed in the notes.

The book is made of oracles, with no clear break after 3:5. Chapters 1-3 are about the marriage, 4-11 are about the LORD's case against Israel, and 12-14 are a closing group that includes a call to return. Whether the closing chapter was written to end the whole book is an open question.

The Hebrew text of Hosea is hard and probably damaged in several places (4:4, 4:18, 5:2, 6:5, 7:4-7, 9:8, 10:10, 11:7, 13:14). The Greek translation differs often, and the Dead Sea scrolls preserve only parts of the book and mostly agree with the Masoretic Text, though 4Q82 has shorter readings at 2:23, 3:3 and 3:5. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text and says where it departs.
outline: The heading: Hosea, five kings
Hosea marries Gomer; three children, Jezreel, Not Shown Compassion and Not My People
The promise that reverses the names
The case against the mother: Israel as an unfaithful wife
The wilderness, the door of hope, the betrothal and the sowing
Hosea buys back a woman; many days without king or priest, then David their king
The LORD's case against the land: no knowledge of God
The priests, the sacred trees and the hill shrines; leave Ephraim alone
Hear this, priests, Israel and the king's house: a trap at Mizpah
The alarm in Benjamin; the moth, the lion and the LORD's withdrawal
The people's song: come, let us turn back
What can I do with you? Loyal love, not sacrifice; Adam, Gilead, Shechem
The coups of Samaria and the oven
A flat loaf, a silly dove and a slack bow
The trumpet, the kings made without the LORD, the calf of Samaria, sowing the wind
No joy in exile; the prophet a fool, the days of Gibeah
Israel found like grapes in the wilderness; Baal-peor; no children
A luxuriant vine; the calf of Beth-aven; sow righteousness and reap loyal love
When Israel was a youth I loved him; how can I give you away?
Jacob in the womb and in Aram; Ephraim's lies; a prophet brought Israel up from Egypt
Baal and the calves; death and Sheol; Samaria's end
Return to the LORD: bring words with you; I will heal their turning away; the dew

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: The eighth-century northern kingdom: Jeroboam II's peace and the murder of his successors, the Syro-Ephraimite war, Tiglath-pileser III's conquest of Galilee, the vassalage of Menahem and Hoshea, the appeals to Egypt, and the fall of Samaria in 722 BC (2 Kings 14-17). The question is what in the book belongs to which year and what has already come true.

lenses.name: Critical scholarship
lenses.desc: The hard and sometimes damaged Hebrew; the Greek and the Dead Sea scrolls; Judean additions and the composition of the book after 722 BC; the marriage chapters and their relation (1 third person, 3 first); the metaphors of marriage and the feminist critique; sacred prostitution and Baal religion; the Book of the Twelve.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The Targum Jonathan to the Prophets; the Talmud on Hosea and Gomer (Pesachim 87a-b) and Rosh Hashanah 31a on 5:15; Maimonides on prophetic visions; Hosea 2 as the haftarah for Bemidbar and Hosea 14 for Shabbat Shuvah before Yom Kippur; Hosea 2:19-20 at the binding of the tefillin. This site has not checked the Rashi, Ibn Ezra or Kimhi commentaries on Hosea 1-7, so none is attributed a view in those chapters.

lenses.name: Christian tradition
lenses.desc: The New Testament uses (Matthew 2:15; 9:13; 12:7; Romans 9:25-26; 1 Corinthians 15:55; 1 Peter 2:10); Jerome's Commentary on the Twelve and Cyril of Alexandria on 3:5 and 6:2; the lectionary; the church as the bride and the typology of Israel's exodus. This site has not checked Theodore, Theodoret, Luther, Calvin or Pusey on Hosea 1-7, so none is attributed a view in those chapters.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: The restoration of Israel (3:4-5; 14), the reunion of Judah and Israel (1:11), the covenant with the animals and the end of war (2:18), the resurrection of 6:2 and 13:14, and Paul's "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26): read as a future event, a pattern fulfilled in Christ and the church, or a hope already partly met in the return from exile.

sections.b: Hosea has no table of contents, and the oracles run into one another. Chapters 1-3 are the marriage: the three children (1), the lawsuit and betrothal (2) and the buying of a woman (3). Chapters 4-11 are the case against Israel: priests and shrines (4), the Syro-Ephraimite crisis and the song of return (5-6), the coups and treaties (7-8), exile (9), the vine and the calf (10) and the father who cannot give up his son (11). Chapters 12-14 are a closing group: Jacob and the prophet, death and the grave, and the call to return.

Hosea speaks in pictures, and they come in pairs. Israel is a wife (1-3), a child (11), a vine (10:1), a heifer (4:16), a dove (7:11), a flat loaf (7:8) and a sick man (5:13). The LORD is a husband, a father who taught his son to walk (11:3), a healer (6:1; 14:4), a moth and a lion (5:12, 14), and, in the last chapter, the dew (14:5). The Plain English Translation keeps the images as the Hebrew has them.

The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text, the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex, and says in each case where the Greek, a Dead Sea scroll or a scholarly emendation reads differently. In chapters 1-7 the Plain English Translation follows the Greek over the Masoretic Text only at 6:5 ("my judgment goes out like light"). A reader who sees "uncertain" in a note is seeing the truth: at 4:18, 5:2, 7:4-7 and elsewhere, no one is sure what the Hebrew says.

English Bibles and the Hebrew Bible number some verses differently. In Hosea, English 1:10-11 is Hebrew 2:1-2; English 2:1-23 is Hebrew 2:3-25; English 11:12 is Hebrew 12:1, and English 12:1-14 is Hebrew 12:2-15; English 13:16 is Hebrew 14:1, and English 14:1-9 is Hebrew 14:2-10. This book uses English numbers everywhere and says so in the first affected note. When Jewish sources cite "Hosea 2:21" they mean English 2:19.

sections.h: Hosea in the Jewish year and the New Testament
sections.b: The haftarah for Bemidbar (before Shavuot) is Hosea 2:1-22 in the Hebrew numbering, English 1:10-2:20. The haftarah for Shabbat Shuvah (between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur) is Hosea 14:2-10. The New Testament quotes Hosea 1:10 and 2:23 (Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10), 6:6 (Matthew 9:13; 12:7), 10:8 (Luke 23:30; Revelation 6:16), 11:1 (Matthew 2:15), 13:14 (1 Corinthians 15:55) and 14:2 (Hebrews 13:15, in the Greek form).

Hosea stands first in the Hebrew and the Greek order of the Twelve Prophets. Its heading is dated by kings of both kingdoms, like Amos's, and its themes of judgment, return and loyal love echo through the neighbors. See the topic on the Book of the Twelve for the debate about whether the Twelve were meant as one book.

spec.title: Every picture of failure has a matching picture of healing
spec.body: My own observation, which overlaps with the general view that Hosea 14 answers the rest of the book: nearly every image of Israel's fault finds an answer in the last chapter. The wife who ran after lovers (2:5) is called back (14:4); the child who would not be taught to walk (11:3) is healed (14:4); the "luxuriant vine" whose fruit went to altars (10:1) is answered by the LORD as a luxuriant cypress who says, "your fruit comes from me" (14:8); the lion (5:14) and the moth (5:12) give way to the dew (14:5). If this is deliberate, the closing chapter is not an add-on but a reply, point for point, to the charges. It rests on 2:5, 5:12, 5:14, 10:1, 11:3 and 14:4-8 and cannot be proved.

prompts: A drawing sketched onto a scroll in ink and ochre: a man in a plain robe kneeling in a field, three children walking beside a woman, each child carrying a small tablet with a single Hebrew word, in the manner of an ancient manuscript mixed with cave drawing and modern line art, soft hand-drawn edges, no hard rectangle.

A dry valley of rocks drawn in charcoal and red ochre, with a small arched doorway in the hillside at its end and light coming through it, a woman's silhouette walking toward it, sketched on old parchment with torn soft edges.

A round flat loaf of bread on hot stones, burnt black on its upper face and pale on the other, with a dove and a bow nearby, drawn like a cave painting and modern sketch together, uneven edges and warm earth colors.

On one half of a scroll, a lion with its mouth open, in rough ink lines; on the other half, a field of lilies and a cedar under early dew, in soft green washes, the two halves joined without a hard border.
reading: The great critical commentary on the Hebrew, strong on the growth of the book and the setting of each oracle.
Francis I. Andersen and David Noel Freedman, Hosea (Anchor Bible)
A very full commentary with close attention to the text, the language and the structure of the book.
James Luther Mays, Hosea (Old Testament Library)
A shorter, clear commentary with a theological reading of the book's images.
An evangelical commentary that takes the marriage as real and gives the covenant background.
J. Andrew Dearman, The Book of Hosea (NICOT)
A recent commentary that discusses the marriage, the metaphors and the critique.
Gale Yee, Hosea (in The Women's Bible Commentary)
A short critical reading of the book's picture of women.
A defense of the marriage metaphor within the Bible's theology of covenant.
